reasons.hook_strength: Opens a specific, honest question for someone about to send a note link: what does the reader actually see? The planned payoff (open the generated URL in a signed-out private window) answers it directly. The hook is slightly generic, but it is not misleading.
reasons.clarity_2s: 'Skwirl note link' plus the Share control visible in the owner view makes the subject and the promise clear in the first frame. The audience (friends swapping tips) matches the send trigger.
reasons.payoff: The planned shot is concrete and filmable: click the real Share control, show the generated URL, open it signed out, and show the read-only page and its content. That backs 'anyone with this link can read this note' from note_share's implementation evidence (public read-only GET /n/<share_id>). The limit beat adds little new information, but it is honest and neutral, with no fictional leak animation.
reasons.originality: No sharing or reader-view piece exists in the supplied history. The existing items are search, recipes, lists, depth and carousels. The structure (owner view, then signed-out reader view) is distinct from the tutorials and POVs already there, and the difference is more than lexical.
reasons.brand_fit: Plain, calm and useful, with no hype, invented numbers or testimonial. It states the permission limit instead of selling around it, and the CTA is a simple 'Try Skwirl. Link in bio.'

reasons.hook_strength: 'You shared a note link. Can you take it back?' states a real worry as an honest question. Slides 4 and 5 answer it, and the slide 1 bridge ('Yes for the link. Not for everything.') signals the qualified answer. It is specific to people who share notes by link and does not rely on a number or a trick.
reasons.clarity_2s: Within two seconds the viewer knows the subject is a shared note link and whether it can be revoked. The first frame is bold type with a link icon. Skwirl is not named until slide 2, which is acceptable for a hook slide.
reasons.payoff: The payoff is a planned, filmable demonstration. It shows the stop-sharing control, then the in-app message, then the old link opened in a browser. The in-app message is backed by the source anchor 'Stopped sharing. The old link no longer works.' The limit slide states what it cannot undo, which closes the question honestly. Slide 3 is thin, but it is supported by a real capture.
reasons.originality: Nothing in the supplied history (ideas backlog, handbook pieces, captions) covers sharing a note by link or revoking it. The angle of what revoking can and cannot undo is new for this account. The slide structure is conventional, but the topic and the limit-first honesty are distinct.
reasons.brand_fit: The voice is plain and useful. There is no hype, no invented numbers, and no guarantee. The limit is stated openly, and the demo is labelled as a seeded demo with no real names. The CTA is simple.

claim_audit.text: Yes for the link. Not for everything.

reasons.hook_strength: "Can you take your notes out of Skwirl?" is a direct ownership question for people who want their own notes. The payoff answers it with a real download and an opened file, so the question is honestly resolved. It is plain rather than exceptional, so 4 and not 5.
reasons.clarity_2s: The subject (Skwirl notes, getting them out) is clear from the first-frame text and VO in about two seconds. The first shot is a seeded library at Me with no private data visible.
reasons.payoff: The planned demonstration is filmable and supported. It clicks Export my notes, shows the skwirl-export.json download, opens it in a text editor and highlights title, summary and note text on one controlled note. This matches the schema evidence (NOTE_COLUMNS plus markdown, wrapped as {exported_at, notes}). The limit beat says copy of notes, not videos, and the shot excludes PDF, backup and import icons.
reasons.originality: No history item covers export of notes. The nearest items, I-07 and the import carousel, are about importing Instagram saves, which is a different direction and a different promise. The open-the-file proof structure is distinct from earlier tours and POV pieces.
reasons.brand_fit: The voice is plain and useful, and the limits are stated honestly (notes, not videos). It has no hype, no invented numbers and no testimonial. The CTA is a simple Try Skwirl, link in bio.

reasons.hook_strength: 'Signal dropped. Can you still read your note?' names an everyday moment for travellers and people on weak signal. It opens an honest question, and the 'Sometimes. Here are the conditions.' bridge keeps that honesty. Slide 4 answers it and slides 5 and 6 bound the answer, so the payoff matches the promise. The hook has no product name, which is a minor weakness.
reasons.clarity_2s: Signal, note and reading are clear from the first frame, and the weak-signal-bar-over-a-note visual reinforces them. Skwirl is not named until slide 4, but the account branding and the stated audience cover this. The hook is plain, short and unambiguous.
reasons.payoff: Slide 4 specifies a concrete, filmable demonstration: a real capture on a seeded demo account, a note open, connection turned off, and the cached note still readable. That is supported by the offline_notes source (kept.byId fallback). Slides 5 and 6 state the scope and open limits, and no cold-start or new-save processing claim is made. The planned demonstration is possible and specific.
reasons.originality: No history entry covers offline or cached reading. The nearest items are the I-01 'can disappear' carousel and the Saved-folder graveyard posts. The myth-bust structure (belief, condition, demonstration, limits) is distinct from the posted launch, graveyard, fridge and books pieces. The angle is a limits-forward answer rather than a feature tour.
reasons.brand_fit: The voice is plain and useful, with no hype, no guarantee and no invented numbers. The scope limits are stated up front. The CTA is a simple 'Try Skwirl. Link in bio.' and the hashtags are modest and relevant.

claim_audit.text: While Skwirl stays open, you can read notes already cached on this device if the connection drops. Do not expect it to start fresh with no signal, or new saves to process.
claim_audit.reason: The first sentence matches the approved offline_notes copy verbatim. The second sentence states the limits (no cold start offline, no new-save processing), which the feature limits require.

reasons.hook_strength: Frame zero shows a mismatched category on a labelled demo note and asks 'wrong category? Fix it on the note.' The question is specific and the two-tap payoff answers it directly. The 'Skwirl Plus demo:' prefix is a little label-heavy, but it discloses both the entitlement and the staging.
reasons.clarity_2s: The subject is clear in two seconds: a note, a visibly wrong Food category, and a fix. The shot plan pairs the craft title with the wrong chip, so the problem reads without voiceover.
reasons.payoff: Beat 2 plans a real capture of tapping the wrong category off and the right existing one on, in the current UI. Beat 3 shows the chips updating, which matches the toggle-and-post handler in the evidence. The shots are filmable and supported. The staged mismatch is honestly labelled and not presented as a model error.
reasons.originality: History has nothing on manual category correction. The closest items are the categories/work-library idea (I-10) and the Plus static (I-09), and neither is a fix-it-yourself demo. The do-dont structure is distinct from the recipe, search and loss-framed pieces already made.
reasons.brand_fit: The copy is plain and useful. It states the limits (existing categories only, manual fix) and avoids 'Plus only' and any accuracy promise. It uses no invented numbers and no testimonial.
